title: Site Reliability Engineer
tagline: Keep large systems fast and available using software engineering.
about: Site Reliability Engineering, pioneered at Google, applies software engineering to operations. SREs define reliability targets, build automation to remove toil, run incident response and design systems that degrade gracefully.
It needs strong coding plus deep systems knowledge, and usually comes after experience in backend or DevOps work.
day: Define SLOs and error budgets with product teams
Build automation that removes manual work
Respond to and learn from incidents
Do capacity planning and load testing

nodes.d: Users, permissions, processes, services and package management on a real server.
links: OverTheWire: Bandit (learn the shell by playing)

links: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT)

nodes.d: IP, DNS, TCP, HTTP, TLS, load balancers and firewalls: what you'll debug every week.
Everything in infrastructure is versioned: code, config and infrastructure definitions.
Python or Go for tooling, automation and glue code.

project.d: Rent a small VPS, harden SSH, set up a firewall, serve a site over HTTPS with NGINX and automatic certificate renewal, and document every step in a README.

phases.title: Systems depth

nodes.d: Find bottlenecks with the right tools and methods.

links: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (free book)

nodes.d: How the platform schedules, restarts and isolates workloads.
Measure reliability the way users experience it and decide how much risk to take.
Metrics, logs and traces that answer new questions.

Learn from failure without blame, and track follow-ups.

project.d: Instrument a service, define two SLOs, build burn-rate alerts and a dashboard, then run a simulated incident and write the postmortem.

nodes.d: Know your limits before users find them.
Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers and graceful degradation.
Inject failure deliberately to build confidence.

project.d: Load-test a service until it breaks, add timeouts, retries and load shedding, then run a game day and document how behaviour improved.
